label: Chapter 4: Revolt, Bombardment and Reinvention, 1568 to 1795

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the Netherlands of the sixteenth century is a powder keg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the spark comes from Spain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip the Second sent troops and a harsh general, the Duke of Alba, to put down any sign of rebellion.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Alba set up a special court in Brussels that the locals called the Council of Blood, which tried thousands of people for heresy and treason.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it caught some very prominent people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two of the most prominent noblemen in the country, the Count of Egmont and the Count of Hoorn.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Both were Catholics, loyal subjects who had only asked the king to show some moderation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It made no difference.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened to them?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the fifth of June, 1568, Egmont and Hoorn were beheaded on a scaffold in front of the town hall on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The execution shocked the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Egmont became a martyr, and in later centuries his story inspired a play by Goethe and an overture by Beethoven.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And politically?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It helped turn a local protest into a full-scale war, the Eighty Years' War.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The revolt was long and bloody.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the north, the Dutch provinces under William of Orange eventually broke away and formed the Dutch Republic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the south, the fighting seesawed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels itself joined the rebels and, for a few years in the fifteen-seventies and fifteen-eighties, was run by a militant Calvinist regime.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But in 1585, a Spanish army under the Duke of Parma retook Brussels after a long siege.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which had consequences far beyond Brussels, I think.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many Protestants fled north, taking their skills and their money with them, and they helped build the great Dutch cities of the seventeenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The southern Netherlands, including Brussels, stayed under Spanish control and stayed Catholic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A border had been drawn through the Low Countries, and it's roughly the border between Belgium and the Netherlands today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Did Brussels recover under the Spanish?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Slowly. From 1598 to 1621, the southern Netherlands were governed by a popular and cultured couple, the Archduke Albert and the Archduchess Isabella, who made Brussels a glittering capital again.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Their court attracted artists, including the great Peter Paul Rubens, who painted for them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A wave of baroque churches and palaces rose across the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It sounds like a golden age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It looked like one. But Spain was declining, and a new threat was rising in the south: France, under King Louis the Fourteenth, the Sun King.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Louis wanted to expand France's frontiers to the north and east, and the Spanish Netherlands lay right in his path.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For decades, French armies marched back and forth across the region, and the country suffered from endless war.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then 1695.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The worst blow fell in August of 1695, during a conflict called the Nine Years' War.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A French army of tens of thousands, under Marshal Villeroi, marched on Brussels, not to capture it, but to punish it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Punish it? Why?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The French wanted to draw their enemies away from another city under siege, the fortress of Namur.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels was a rich city that was poorly defended, so it made a tempting target.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the evening of the thirteenth of August, French cannons and mortars began to fire red-hot shot and incendiary shells into the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bombardment went on for about two days and nights.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The spire of the Town Hall was the obvious target, since it was the tallest landmark, and the shells rained down around it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the streets were narrow and medieval.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So fires spread. When it was over, about a third of the buildings in Brussels had been destroyed or badly damaged.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Grand Place was in ruins. All that remained of the town hall was the shell of its stone walls, still standing, the spire miraculously intact.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It must have been terrible.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the most destructive event in the city's long history.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The warning had been sent ahead, so the casualties were far fewer than they might have been, but the damage to property was staggering.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And now the part I love, because what happened next is the best part of the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. The people of Brussels did not despair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They didn't abandon the center, and they didn't rebuild on a new plan.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Instead, the guilds, which owned the plots around the Grand Place, set to work.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city council and the governor required that every plan be submitted for approval, which meant that the new buildings would fit together.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How long did it take?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within about four years, the square had risen again, in stone this time rather than wood.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Each guildhall was a showpiece, decked with gilded statues, carvings, and symbols of its trade.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So you can read the trades on the facades.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The butchers, the bakers, the brewers, the boatmen, the cabinet-makers, and the painters.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The house that belonged to the guild of the boatmen has a gable shaped like a ship's stern.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Another crowned its roofline with a golden phoenix, rising from the flames, as a symbol of the rebirth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And all those different styles side by side.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Gothic, baroque, and Louis the Fourteenth styles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The mixture shouldn't work, but it does, and in 1998, UNESCO placed the Grand Place on its World Heritage list.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then we move into the eighteenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Spanish Habsburg line died out, and after a long war of succession, the southern Netherlands passed to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1714.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the next eighty years, Brussels was the capital of the Austrian Netherlands, and the country enjoyed a long period of relative peace and prosperity.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who was the beloved ruler?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Charles of Lorraine, a brother-in-law of the Empress Maria Theresa, who governed from 1744 to 1780.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A genial, sociable man who loved hunting, science, and a good table.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And under him the city gets a makeover.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the elegant neoclassical style.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1731, the old Coudenberg Palace had been destroyed by a fire, and its ruins were cleared away and covered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In its place, the authorities built a handsome new district: the Place Royale, a harmonious square lined with uniform facades, and a park laid out in geometric patterns, now the Parc de Bruxelles, with straight avenues and statues.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which are among the most graceful spaces in the city today.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they date from this period.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the old order was about to crack.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Enlightenment had arrived, and the Emperor Joseph the Second, who ruled from Vienna from 1780, tried to modernize his lands at breakneck speed, closing monasteries, reorganizing the courts, and curbing the power of the church.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And people didn't like it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many in the Austrian Netherlands, who loved their ancient privileges, were furious.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1789, the year the French Revolution began, a rebellion broke out in Brabant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It drove the Austrians out, and in January of 1790 a new state, the United Belgian States, was proclaimed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The first time the word Belgian appears in a country's name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the republic quickly collapsed in quarrels between conservatives and democrats, and the Austrians returned in December of 1790.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then France arrives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did not last long, the Austrians.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1792, French revolutionary armies marched in, and after a few years of back and forth, they won a decisive victory in 1794.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1795, France formally annexed the southern Netherlands, as it did the Duchy of Luxembourg, which became the Department of the Forests.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels became the capital of a French department called the Dyle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The old privileges of the Joyous Entry were swept away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The ancien régime was gone, and Brussels, like the rest of what would become Belgium, was now part of a new France.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next time, Napoleon, Waterloo, and a night at the opera that changed the map of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which sounds like a joke, but isn't.
